rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the reactions is used in the conversion of a ketone into hydrocarbon ?
rows.solution:
Wolff-Kishner reduction converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), so a ketone becomes a hydrocarbon. The ketone is first condensed with hydrazine to give the hydrazone, which is then heated with a strong base such as potassium hydroxide in ethylene glycol; nitrogen is expelled and only the hydrocarbon remains:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{C{=}N-NH_2} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{glycol}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)
Reimer-Tiemann puts a \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group onto phenol, aldol condensation joins two carbonyl molecules, and the Stephen reaction makes an aldehyde from a nitrile — none of them removes the oxygen. Clemmensen reduction, with zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid, achieves the same conversion in acidic conditions.

rows.stem:
Which of the following reagents are used to prepare primary amines by Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction ?
(i) \(\mathrm{R-CO-NH_2}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\)
(iv) \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\)
rows.solution:
Hofmann bromamide degradation treats an amide with bromine in aqueous or alcoholic ALKALI, so three things are needed: the amide itself, bromine, and sodium hydroxide.
\(\mathrm{R-CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
So the reagents are (i), (ii) and (iii). Chloroform belongs to the carbylamine test, a different reaction that DETECTS a primary amine rather than preparing one, so (iv) has no place here.

rows.stem: The major product of carbylamine reaction is :
rows.solution:
In the carbylamine reaction a primary amine is warmed with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide. The alkali generates dichlorocarbene, which the amine's nitrogen attacks, and after loss of hydrogen chloride the product is an isocyanide:
\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The isocyanide's foul smell is what makes this a test. Note that it is the isocyanide, \(\mathrm{R-NC}\), and not the isomeric cyanide \(\mathrm{R-CN}\), that forms — the nitrogen, not the carbon, was the nucleophile.

rows.stem: Actinoids show larger number of oxidation states :

options.label: A
options.text: because they are radioactive in nature

options.label: B
options.text: because they have large atomic numbers

options.label: C
options.text: because they have large atomic masses

options.label: D
options.text: due to comparable energies of 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals

rows.solution:
Actinoids show many oxidation states because their 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals lie very close together in energy, so comparable amounts of energy remove electrons from all three and many different numbers of electrons can be lost. Uranium alone runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\).

The other suggestions describe true facts that explain nothing here. Radioactivity is a property of the nucleus and has no bearing on valence electrons, and large atomic number or atomic mass by itself does not produce variable valency.

rows.stem:
Consider the following reaction and identify A and B :
\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl + NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \mathrm{A + B}\)
rows.solution:
This is the Finkelstein reaction. Sodium iodide is soluble in dry acetone but sodium chloride is not, so as the iodide displaces the chloride the sodium chloride precipitates out and is removed from the equilibrium, driving the reaction forward:
\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)
So A is iodomethane and B is sodium chloride. Note that the solvent must be dry, since water would let the sodium chloride dissolve and the reaction would not go to completion.

rows.stem: The correct formula of Hinsberg’s reagent is :
rows.solution: Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\). It is used to tell the three classes of amine apart: with a primary amine the sulphonamide formed still has an acidic hydrogen on nitrogen and dissolves in alkali; with a secondary amine no hydrogen is left, so the sulphonamide is insoluble in alkali; and a tertiary amine does not react at all. Benzoyl chloride is the reagent of the Schotten-Baumann reaction, and neither of the remaining formulae is an acid chloride.

rows.stem: Half-life \(\mathrm{(t_{1/2})}\) of a first order reaction is 1386 s. The value of rate constant is :
rows.solution:
For a first order reaction the half-life is independent of the starting concentration and is related to the rate constant by
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

Rearranging,
\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1386} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

The units confirm the order: a first order rate constant can only carry reciprocal time.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following ligands forms a chelate complex ?
rows.solution: A chelate forms when one ligand grips the metal through two or more donor atoms at once, closing a ring. That requires a polydentate ligand. Ammonia and water each have only one donor atom, so both are monodentate. The nitrite ion has two different donor atoms but uses only one of them at a time — it is ambidentate, not bidentate. The oxalate ion binds through two oxygen atoms simultaneously, forming a five-membered ring with the metal, so it is the one that gives a chelate complex.

rows.stem: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols can be distinguished by :
rows.solution:
The Lucas test distinguishes all three classes. Lucas reagent is concentrated hydrochloric acid with anhydrous zinc chloride, and the cloudiness that appears is the insoluble alkyl chloride. Because the reaction goes through a carbocation, the timing separates the classes: a tertiary alcohol turns the mixture cloudy at once, a secondary alcohol takes about five minutes, and a primary alcohol gives no cloudiness at room temperature.

Fehling's and Tollens' tests are for aldehydes, and Hinsberg's test is for amines, so none of those three can be used on alcohols at all.

rows.stem:
Consider the following compounds :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)
The correct increasing order of the above compounds on the basis of their basic strength is :
rows.solution:
Three influences set the order. Alkyl groups release electron density onto nitrogen and raise basicity, which puts the diethylamine above ethylamine. Attaching nitrogen directly to a benzene ring delocalises its lone pair into the ring and lowers basicity sharply, which puts aniline below even ammonia. And inserting a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group between the ring and the nitrogen, as in benzylamine, breaks that conjugation, so benzylamine behaves as an ordinary aliphatic amine — stronger than ammonia but weaker than ethylamine, whose alkyl group is directly attached and donates more effectively.

The increasing order of basic strength is therefore
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2NH_2} < \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} < (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH}\)

rows.stem: Identify the polysaccharide among the following :
rows.solution: Cellulose is the polysaccharide: it is a long chain of glucose units joined by \(\beta\)-1,4 glycosidic linkages, and it does not taste sweet or dissolve in water, as polysaccharides do not. Fructose and glucose are monosaccharides, single sugar units that cannot be hydrolysed further, and maltose is a disaccharide of two glucose units.

rows.stem: The polypeptide chain in a protein has amino acids linked with each other in a specific sequence. This specific sequence of amino acids is called :
rows.solution:
The primary structure of a protein is the sequence in which its amino acid residues are joined along the chain. Change one residue in that sequence and the protein becomes a different protein, which is why the primary structure is the most fundamental level.

The secondary structure is how the chain folds locally into an \(\alpha\)-helix or a \(\beta\)-pleated sheet; the tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of the whole chain; and the quaternary structure describes how several separate chains assemble, as the four subunits of haemoglobin do.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : D (+) – Glucose is dextrorotatory in nature.
Reason (R) : (+) represents dextrorotatory nature and D represents the configuration.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
D-(+)-glucose is dextrorotatory, so the Assertion is true. The Reason explains what the two symbols mean, and its account is correct: the \((+)\) sign records the direction of optical rotation, measured experimentally, while the capital D records the configuration at the chiral carbon farthest from the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group, compared with (+)-glyceraldehyde.

Since it is precisely the \((+)\) symbol that asserts dextrorotation, the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion. Worth adding: the two symbols are independent, and a D compound need not be dextrorotatory — D-(−)-fructose is the standing counterexample.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Highest oxidation state of Mn is +7 in first series of transition elements.
Reason (R) : Transition metals exhibit variable oxidation states.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Manganese does show \(+7\), the highest oxidation state in the first transition series, so the Assertion is true. Transition metals do show variable oxidation states, so the Reason is true as well.

But the Reason is too general to explain the Assertion. Why the maximum is \(+7\) for MANGANESE specifically follows from its configuration \(3d^5 4s^2\): seven electrons in the two outermost subshells, and the maximum oxidation state is reached when all of them are used. So both are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : p-nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol.
Reason (R) : Nitro group is an electron-withdrawing group, it stabilises phenoxide ion by dispersal of negative charge.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: p-Nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason gives exactly the right mechanism. Acidity is decided by how stable the phenoxide ion is once the proton has left. The nitro group withdraws electron density both inductively and by resonance, and from the para position it can take the negative charge onto its own oxygen atoms. Dispersing the charge in this way stabilises the phenoxide, so the proton comes off more readily. The Reason is therefore the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : All aliphatic aldehydes give a positive Fehling’s test.
Reason (R) : Aliphatic aldehydes are reduced by Fehling’s reagent.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
All aliphatic aldehydes do give a positive Fehling's test — a red-brown precipitate of cuprous oxide — so the Assertion is true. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde do not, which is what the word aliphatic is doing in the statement.

The Reason reverses the chemistry. In that test the ALDEHYDE is oxidised, to the carboxylate, while Fehling's reagent is REDUCED, the copper going from \(+2\) to \(+1\). Saying the aldehyde is reduced by the reagent has the roles the wrong way round. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem:
\(1{\cdot}00\) molal aqueous solution of trichloroacetic acid is heated to its boiling point. Boiling point of this solution was found to be \(100{\cdot}18^\circ\)C. Calculate the van’t Hoff factor for trichloroacetic acid.
(Given : \(\mathrm{K_b}\) for water = \(0{\cdot}512\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of what is observed to what the formula alone would predict:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{observed colligative property}}{\text{calculated colligative property}}\)

The observed elevation is
\(\Delta T_b(\text{observed}) = 100.18 - 100 = 0.18\ \mathrm{K}\)

and the value expected if there were no association or dissociation is
\(\Delta T_b(\text{calculated}) = K_b \times m = 0.512 \times 1.00 = 0.512\ \mathrm{K}\)

So
\(i = \dfrac{0.18}{0.512} = 0.3516\)

A factor well BELOW 1 means the solute has associated: fewer particles are present than the formula suggests. Trichloroacetic acid molecules are dimerising in solution here, not dissociating.

rows.stem:
State Henry’s law. Calculate the mole fraction of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in water at 298 K under 760 mm Hg.
(Given : \(\mathrm{K_H}\) for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) at 298 K = \(1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{6}\) mm Hg)
rows.solution:
Henry's law states that at a given temperature the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid. Written in terms of mole fraction,
\(p = K_H\,x\)

where \(K_H\) is Henry's constant for that gas and solvent. Rearranging and substituting,
\(x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dfrac{p}{K_H} = \dfrac{760}{1.25 \times 10^{6}}\)
\(x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 6.08 \times 10^{-4}\)

Both quantities must be in the same pressure unit, which they are here — millimetres of mercury — so no conversion is needed and the mole fraction comes out dimensionless, as it must.

rows.stem:
(a) Name the cell which was used in the Apollo space programme for providing electrical power.
(b) Define limiting molar conductivity.
rows.solution:
(a) The hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. It was chosen for the Apollo space programme because it converts chemical energy to electricity directly and at high efficiency, and because its only product is water, which the crew could drink.

(b) Limiting molar conductivity, \(\Lambda^{\circ}_m\), is the molar conductivity of an electrolyte solution in the limit of infinite dilution, that is the value \(\Lambda_m\) approaches as the concentration approaches zero. At that limit the ions are so far apart that they no longer influence one another.

rows.stem:
(a) Complete the following equation :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^{+}Cl^{-} + C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{OH^{-}}}\)
(b) How will you convert nitromethane to methyl isocyanide ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a) is printed as a DRAWN structural equation, not as text: a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{N_2^{+}Cl^{-}}\), plus a second benzene ring drawn with its PARA hydrogen shown explicitly (‘H—’) and an OH on the opposite carbon, over an \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) arrow. Both compounds are named losslessly in the stem as benzenediazonium chloride and phenol, so the row is answerable from text — but the explicit para-H is a positional cue that exists only in the drawing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) This is a coupling reaction. In mildly alkaline solution the benzenediazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile and attacks the strongly activated ring of phenol, at the position para to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-OH\ (p)} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
The product is p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye. Azo coupling of this kind is the basis of a whole class of dyes.

(b) Two steps. Reduce the nitro compound to the primary amine with tin and hydrochloric acid, then apply the carbylamine reaction, treating that amine with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide:
\(\mathrm{CH_3NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{alc. }\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3NC}\)

rows.stem:
(a) What are the products obtained on hydrolysis of sucrose ?
(b) What are essential amino acids ?
rows.solution:
(a) Sucrose is a disaccharide of one glucose unit and one fructose unit, so hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose and D-(−)-fructose in equal amounts. The mixture is called invert sugar, because the sign of the rotation changes during the hydrolysis: sucrose is dextrorotatory, but fructose is so strongly laevorotatory that the product mixture rotates to the left.

(b) Essential amino acids are those the body cannot synthesise for itself and must therefore obtain ready-made from the diet. Valine, leucine and lysine are examples. The rest, which the body can make, are called non-essential.

rows.stem:
(a) Write any two fat soluble vitamins.
(b) How will you confirm the presence of five – OH groups in a glucose molecule, which are attached to different carbon atoms ?
rows.solution:
(a) Vitamin A and vitamin D. Vitamins E and K are equally good answers; all four are fat soluble and are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue, which is why an excess of them can be harmful in a way an excess of the water-soluble vitamins is not.

(b) Treat glucose with acetic anhydride. It gives a stable pentaacetate, that is a derivative carrying exactly five acetyl groups, and since acetylation occurs at hydroxyl groups there must be five of them:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)
That the five sit on five DIFFERENT carbons follows from the derivative being stable: two hydroxyl groups on one carbon would form a gem-diol, which loses water at once.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Cr\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)}\ (0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\ (0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Fe\,(s)}\)
(Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = -\,0{\cdot}74\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = -\,0{\cdot}44\) V, [log 10 = 1])
rows.solution:
Chromium is written on the left, so it is the anode and is oxidised; iron is the cathode.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = (-0.44) - (-0.74) = 0.30\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing electrons — chromium gives up three each, iron takes two each — the cell reaction is
\(2\mathrm{Cr(s)} + 3\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{Fe(s)}\)
so six electrons are transferred and \(n = 6\).

By the Nernst equation,
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 0.30 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(10^{-1})^2}{(10^{-2})^3} = 0.30 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log 10^{4}\)
\(= 0.30 - \dfrac{0.059}{6} \times 4 = 0.30 - 0.0393\)
\(= 0.2606\ \mathrm{V}\), about \(0.26\ \mathrm{V}\)

The exponents in the reaction quotient come from the BALANCED cell reaction, not from the cell diagram, which is where this calculation is most often lost.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) Define order of a reaction.
(b) The rate for the following reaction is given by : \(\mathrm{A + B \rightarrow C}\)
Rate = \(\mathrm{k[A][B]^{2}}\)
(i) How is the rate of reaction affected if we double the concentration of B ?
(ii) Write the overall order of a reaction if ‘A’ is present in large excess.
rows.solution:
(a) The order of a reaction is the sum of the powers to which the concentration terms are raised in the experimentally determined rate law expression.

(b)(i) The rate depends on \([\mathrm{B}]^2\), so doubling the concentration of B multiplies the rate by \(2^2\): the rate becomes four times as large.

(ii) If A is present in large excess its concentration hardly changes as the reaction proceeds, so it can be treated as constant and absorbed into the rate constant. The rate law \(k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2\) becomes \(k'[\mathrm{B}]^2\), and the reaction behaves as second order overall — a pseudo second order reaction.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of the chemical reaction doubles when the temperature is raised from 298 K to 308 K. Calculate activation energy \(\mathrm{(E_a)}\) for this reaction assuming that it does not change with temperature.
(Given : R = \(8{\cdot}314\) J \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{K^{-1}}\), log 2 = \(0{\cdot}30\))
rows.solution:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)\)

The rate doubles, so \(k_2/k_1 = 2\) and the left side is \(\log 2 = 0.30\). With \(T_1 = 298\) K and \(T_2 = 308\) K,
\(\dfrac{1}{298} - \dfrac{1}{308} = \dfrac{308 - 298}{298 \times 308} = \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}\)

so
\(0.30 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308} = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.30 \times 19.147 \times 298 \times 308}{10}\)
\(E_a = 52722\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(52.722\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The unit is part of the answer; the marking scheme deducts half a mark if it is wrong or missing.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{K_3[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]}\)
(b) Differentiate between homoleptic complex and heterolyptic complex.
(c) Which type of isomerism is exhibited by the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Three potassium ions contribute \(+3\), so the complex anion is \(-3\). Three oxalate ligands contribute \(-6\), which leaves chromium at \(+3\). The complex is the anion, so chromium takes the \(-ate\) ending. The name is potassium trioxalatochromate(III).

(b) In a homoleptic complex the metal is bound to only one kind of donor group, as in \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\), where all six ligands are ammonia. In a heteroleptic complex the metal is bound to more than one kind, as in \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+}}\), which carries both ammine and chlorido ligands.

(c) \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) exhibits geometrical isomerism, that is cis-trans isomerism. It is square planar, so the two chlorido ligands may sit adjacent to each other or opposite each other. The cis isomer is the anticancer drug cisplatin, and the trans isomer is inactive — a case where the isomerism matters a great deal.

rows.stem:
(a) A coordination compound \(\mathrm{CrCl_3 \cdot 6H_2O}\) is mixed with excess of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, two moles of AgCl are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the coordination compound.
(b) Write the oxidation state and hybridisation of the central metal in the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\)  [Atomic number of Fe = 26]
(c) Why is \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) coloured ? [Atomic number of Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
(a) Two moles of silver chloride per mole of compound means only two of the three chlorides are free in solution, so the third must be inside the coordination sphere. With six positions to fill and one taken by that chloride, five water molecules complete the sphere, and the sixth water is left outside as water of crystallisation:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_5Cl]Cl_2 \cdot H_2O}\)

(b) In \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) the six water ligands are neutral, so the whole \(+3\) charge belongs to the metal: the oxidation state of iron is \(+3\), and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\). Water is a weak field ligand, so it does not pair those five electrons; all five \(3d\) orbitals stay singly occupied and none is available for bonding. The complex must therefore use outer orbitals, and the hybridisation is \(sp^3d^2\) — an outer orbital, high spin, octahedral complex.

(c) Nickel is \(+2\) here, so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\) and has two unpaired electrons in a partly filled d subshell. The six water ligands split those d orbitals into two sets of different energy, and an electron can absorb a photon of visible light to jump from the lower set to the upper one. This d-d transition removes part of the visible spectrum, and the complex appears in the complementary colour — green for the hexaaquanickel(II) ion.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
How do you convert the following ?
(a) Acetophenone to Benzoic acid
(b) Acetonitrile to Acetone
(c) Benzoic acid to Benzene
rows.solution:
(a) Acetophenone to benzoic acid. The \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group attached to the ring responds to the iodoform reaction: sodium hydroxide with iodine cleaves the methyl group away as iodoform, and acidification liberates the acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH}/\mathrm{I_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

(b) Acetonitrile to acetone. A Grignard reagent adds across the carbon-nitrogen triple bond, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives the ketone; a methyl Grignard supplies the second methyl group.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

(c) Benzoic acid to benzene. Convert the acid to its sodium salt and then heat that with soda lime, a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide; the carboxyl group leaves as carbonate and the ring is left behind.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH}/\mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{C_6H_6}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their acidic strengths :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH}\)
(ii) Why is \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) more reactive than acetone towards reaction with HCN ?
(iii) Complete the equation :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + NH_2-NH_2 \xrightarrow{H^{+}}}\)
rows.solution:
(i) Acidity rises as the group attached withdraws more electron density from the carboxylate ion left behind, and it falls as that group releases electron density. It also matters how FAR the withdrawing group sits from the carboxyl group, since the inductive effect falls off sharply with distance.

The isopropyl compound has only an electron-releasing alkyl group and is the weakest. Of the two bromo acids, the one with bromine on the carbon next to the carboxyl group — the \(\alpha\) position — is stronger than the one with bromine a carbon further away. So the increasing order of acid strength is
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-COOH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH}\)

(ii) Two reasons, both working the same way. Ethanal has one methyl group on its carbonyl carbon and acetone has two, and each methyl group releases electron density towards that carbon, reducing the positive charge the nucleophile is attracted to. Each methyl group also physically blocks the approach of the cyanide ion. With two such groups acetone is both less electrophilic and more crowded, so ethanal is the more reactive towards \(\mathrm{HCN}\).

(iii) Hydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group and water is eliminated, giving the hydrazone:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{NH_2-NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}N-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: An organic compound with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) forms 2,4-DNP derivative, reduces Tollens’ reagent and undergoes Cannizzaro reaction. On vigorous oxidation it gives Benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid. Identify the compound and write the reactions of compound 2,4-DNP and when it undergoes Cannizzaro reaction.
rows.solution:
Every clue narrows the compound down. A 2,4-DNP derivative means a carbonyl group. Reducing Tollens' reagent makes it an aldehyde, not a ketone. Undergoing Cannizzaro's reaction means it has no \(\alpha\) hydrogen, so the carbon next to the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) must belong to the ring. And vigorous oxidation to benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid shows a second oxidisable substituent ORTHO to the first. With the formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) that substituent is a methyl group.

The compound is 2-methylbenzaldehyde.

With 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine it condenses at the carbonyl, losing water, to give the orange-red hydrazone:
\(\mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2N-NH-C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}CH{=}N-NH-C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

With concentrated alkali it disproportionates, one molecule being oxidised to the salt of the acid and another reduced to the alcohol:
\(2\ \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}COO^-} + \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2OH}\)

rows.stem:
Complete the following equations :
(i) anisole \(\mathrm{(C_6H_5OCH_3)}\) + \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2}]{\text{Anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}}\)
(ii) anisole \(\mathrm{(C_6H_5OCH_3)} \xrightarrow{\text{Conc. } \mathrm{(HNO_3 + H_2SO_4)}}\)
rows.context: Ethers are prepared by the dehydration of alcohols in presence of protic acids at 413 K. Symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers can also be prepared by Williamson synthesis. This reaction involves \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) attack of an alkoxide ion on primary alkyl halide. If a tertiary alkyl halide is used, elimination reaction occurs and an alkene is formed, no ether is formed. C – O bond in ethers are cleaved under drastic conditions with excess of HI. When unsymmetrical ethers react with HI, the alkyl halide is formed from smaller alkyl group. If one of the alkyl group is tertiary, the alkyl halide is formed from the tertiary alkyl group because tertiary alkyl carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Cleavage of alkyl aryl ethers takes place at the alkyl-oxygen bond due to more stable aryl-oxygen bond. The order of reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI > HBr > HCl. Aromatic ethers undergo electrophilic substitution reactions. The alkoxy group attached to the aromatic ring activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho- and para-positions.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — both equations are printed as SKELETAL DRAWINGS: a plain benzene hexagon carrying \(\mathrm{OCH_3}\), and the printed stem names nothing at all (‘Complete the following equations :’). The compound is anisole in both and is named losslessly in the stem, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(i) This is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. The \(-\mathrm{OCH_3}\) group is strongly activating and ortho, para directing, so the methyl group enters at those positions and a mixture of two products is obtained:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2}]{\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \text{2-methylanisole} + \text{4-methylanisole}\)
The para compound is the major product, the ortho position being partly blocked by the methoxy group.

(ii) Nitration follows the same direction, and for the same reason:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3} + \text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \text{2-nitroanisole} + \text{4-nitroanisole}\)

rows.stem: Write the names of alkyl halide and sodium alkoxide used to prepare tert-butyl ethyl ether.
rows.context: Ethers are prepared by the dehydration of alcohols in presence of protic acids at 413 K. Symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers can also be prepared by Williamson synthesis. This reaction involves \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) attack of an alkoxide ion on primary alkyl halide. If a tertiary alkyl halide is used, elimination reaction occurs and an alkene is formed, no ether is formed. C – O bond in ethers are cleaved under drastic conditions with excess of HI. When unsymmetrical ethers react with HI, the alkyl halide is formed from smaller alkyl group. If one of the alkyl group is tertiary, the alkyl halide is formed from the tertiary alkyl group because tertiary alkyl carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Cleavage of alkyl aryl ethers takes place at the alkyl-oxygen bond due to more stable aryl-oxygen bond. The order of reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI > HBr > HCl. Aromatic ethers undergo electrophilic substitution reactions. The alkoxy group attached to the aromatic ring activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho- and para-positions.
rows.solution:
Ethyl halide and sodium tert-butoxide — that is, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5X}\) and \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-ONa}\).

The choice is forced, not arbitrary. Williamson synthesis is an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, so the alkoxide must attack the LESS hindered carbon. Taking the other pairing — sodium ethoxide with a tert-butyl halide — the alkoxide would meet a fully substituted carbon, and instead of substituting it would remove a \(\beta\) hydrogen and eliminate, giving 2-methylpropene rather than the ether.

rows.stem: Anisole on reaction with HI gives phenol and \(\mathrm{CH_3 - I}\) and not methanol and iodobenzene. Justify the statement.
rows.context: Ethers are prepared by the dehydration of alcohols in presence of protic acids at 413 K. Symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers can also be prepared by Williamson synthesis. This reaction involves \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) attack of an alkoxide ion on primary alkyl halide. If a tertiary alkyl halide is used, elimination reaction occurs and an alkene is formed, no ether is formed. C – O bond in ethers are cleaved under drastic conditions with excess of HI. When unsymmetrical ethers react with HI, the alkyl halide is formed from smaller alkyl group. If one of the alkyl group is tertiary, the alkyl halide is formed from the tertiary alkyl group because tertiary alkyl carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Cleavage of alkyl aryl ethers takes place at the alkyl-oxygen bond due to more stable aryl-oxygen bond. The order of reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI > HBr > HCl. Aromatic ethers undergo electrophilic substitution reactions. The alkoxy group attached to the aromatic ring activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho- and para-positions.
rows.solution:
The bond that breaks is decided by which one is weaker. In anisole the oxygen's lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so the \(\mathrm{O-C_6H_5}\) bond acquires partial double bond character and is shorter and stronger than an ordinary single bond. The \(\mathrm{O-CH_3}\) bond has no such reinforcement.

So when the protonated ether is attacked, the iodide ion breaks the weaker \(\mathrm{O-CH_3}\) bond. The methyl group leaves with the iodine and the phenyl group keeps the oxygen:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)
Attack at the ring carbon would also mean a nucleophile attacking an \(sp^2\) carbon of an aromatic ring, which does not happen under these conditions.

rows.stem: Why is C – O – C bond angle in ethers slightly greater than tetrahedral angle ?
rows.context: Ethers are prepared by the dehydration of alcohols in presence of protic acids at 413 K. Symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers can also be prepared by Williamson synthesis. This reaction involves \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) attack of an alkoxide ion on primary alkyl halide. If a tertiary alkyl halide is used, elimination reaction occurs and an alkene is formed, no ether is formed. C – O bond in ethers are cleaved under drastic conditions with excess of HI. When unsymmetrical ethers react with HI, the alkyl halide is formed from smaller alkyl group. If one of the alkyl group is tertiary, the alkyl halide is formed from the tertiary alkyl group because tertiary alkyl carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Cleavage of alkyl aryl ethers takes place at the alkyl-oxygen bond due to more stable aryl-oxygen bond. The order of reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI > HBr > HCl. Aromatic ethers undergo electrophilic substitution reactions. The alkoxy group attached to the aromatic ring activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho- and para-positions.
rows.solution: The \(\mathrm{C-O-C}\) angle in an ether is about \(111^{\circ}\hspace{-2pt}-112^{\circ}\), a little more than the tetrahedral \(109.5^{\circ}\). The oxygen is \(sp^3\) hybridised, so \(109.5^{\circ}\) is the starting point, but the two groups attached to it are bulky alkyl groups rather than single hydrogen atoms. Repulsion between those two groups pushes them apart, widening the angle between them slightly. The effect is the opposite of the one in water, where the two lone pairs squeeze the much smaller hydrogen atoms together to about \(104.5^{\circ}\).

rows.stem:
Predict the products of electrolysis in each of the following :
(i) An aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) with platinum electrodes.
(ii) A concentrated solution of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) with platinum electrodes.
rows.context:
Electrochemistry is the study of the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy. Many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy. In electrolysis, electrical energy is converted directly into chemical energy. The product of an electrolytic reaction depends on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrode used. Oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potential too, affect the products of electrolysis. Electrolysis plays an important role in most people’s daily lives, whether it is for the manufacturing of aluminium, electroplating of metals, or the synthesis of chemical compounds.
Michael Faraday was the first scientist who proposed two laws to explain the quantitative aspects of electrolysis, popularly known as Faraday’s laws of electrolysis. Faraday’s laws of electrolysis provide a basis for mathematical analysis of the mass deposited at electrodes and the amount of charge passed through them.
Faraday’s laws are fundamental in various applications, including electroplating, metal extraction, battery technology and chemical synthesis. These laws also help in environmental monitoring and in various chemistry experiments.
rows.solution:
(i) Aqueous \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) with platinum electrodes. At the cathode copper is deposited, since \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) has a higher reduction potential than water:
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\)
At the anode chlorine is evolved. On standard potentials alone water should be oxidised first, but oxygen evolution on platinum carries a large overpotential, so chloride wins in practice:
\(2\mathrm{Cl^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2} + 2e^-\)

(ii) Concentrated sulphuric acid with platinum electrodes. At the anode the sulphate ions are oxidised to the peroxodisulphate ion:
\(2\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}} + 2e^-\)
At the cathode hydrogen gas is liberated:
\(\mathrm{H_2O} + e^- \longrightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{OH^-}\)

rows.stem: How much charge in faraday is required for the reduction of 1 mol of \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) to Ag ?

rows.solution: One faraday. The reduction \(\mathrm{Ag^+} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}\) needs a single electron per silver ion, so 1 mol of silver ions needs 1 mol of electrons, which is 1 F, or 96500 C.

rows.solution: Faraday's second law of electrolysis states that when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytic solutions, the amounts of the different substances liberated at the electrodes are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights.

rows.stem:
The following reactions occur at the anode during the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride solution :
\(\mathrm{Cl^{-}(aq)} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2(g) + e^{-}}\)   \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{(cell)}} = 1{\cdot}36\) V   (I)
\(\mathrm{2H_2O}\,(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2(g) + 4H^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-}}\)   \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{(cell)}} = 1{\cdot}23\) V   (II)
Which reaction is feasible at the anode and why ?
rows.context:
Electrochemistry is the study of the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy. Many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy. In electrolysis, electrical energy is converted directly into chemical energy. The product of an electrolytic reaction depends on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrode used. Oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potential too, affect the products of electrolysis. Electrolysis plays an important role in most people’s daily lives, whether it is for the manufacturing of aluminium, electroplating of metals, or the synthesis of chemical compounds.
Michael Faraday was the first scientist who proposed two laws to explain the quantitative aspects of electrolysis, popularly known as Faraday’s laws of electrolysis. Faraday’s laws of electrolysis provide a basis for mathematical analysis of the mass deposited at electrodes and the amount of charge passed through them.
Faraday’s laws are fundamental in various applications, including electroplating, metal extraction, battery technology and chemical synthesis. These laws also help in environmental monitoring and in various chemistry experiments.
rows.solution:
Reaction (I) is the one that occurs: chlorine is evolved at the anode.

On the standard potentials alone it should not be. Oxidising water needs \(1.23\) V and oxidising chloride needs \(1.36\) V, so oxygen ought to appear first. What decides it in practice is OVERPOTENTIAL — the extra voltage, over and above the thermodynamic value, that a gas needs in order to be evolved on a real electrode surface. For oxygen that extra requirement is large, so the effective voltage needed to release oxygen exceeds the \(1.36\) V needed for chlorine, and chlorine is produced instead.

This is a case where thermodynamics alone gives the wrong prediction and the kinetics of the electrode process settles the outcome.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the freezing point of a solution when \(10{\cdot}5\) g of \(\mathrm{MgBr_2}\) was dissolved in 250 g of water, assuming \(\mathrm{MgBr_2}\) undergoes complete dissociation.
(Given : Molar mass of \(\mathrm{MgBr_2}\) = 184 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = \(1{\cdot}86\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
(ii) Write two differences between ideal and non-ideal solutions.
rows.solution:
(i) Magnesium bromide dissociates completely into one \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and two \(\mathrm{Br^-}\), so three particles per formula unit and \(i = 3\).

\(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f \times \dfrac{W_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{W_A}\)
\(= 3 \times 1.86 \times \dfrac{10.5}{184} \times \dfrac{1000}{250}\)
\(= 1.27\ \mathrm{K}\)

The depression is subtracted from the freezing point of the pure solvent:
\(T_f = 273.15 - 1.27 = 271.88\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(-1.27\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

(ii) An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the whole range of concentration; a non-ideal solution does not, showing either positive or negative deviation.

For an ideal solution the enthalpy of mixing and the volume of mixing are both zero, \(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\) and \(\Delta V_{mix} = 0\), because the A-B interactions are just as strong as the A-A and B-B ones they replace. For a non-ideal solution neither is zero, since the new interactions differ in strength from the old.

rows.stem:
(i) A solution is prepared by dissolving \(0{\cdot}025\) g of potassium sulphate in 2 L of water at \(27^\circ\)C. Assuming potassium sulphate is completely dissociated, determine its osmotic pressure.
(Given : R = \(0{\cdot}082\) L atm \(\mathrm{K^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), Molar mass of \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) = 174 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
(ii) What type of azeotrope will be formed by a solution of acetone and chloroform ? Give reason.
rows.solution:
(i) Potassium sulphate dissociates completely into two \(\mathrm{K^+}\) and one \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\), so three particles per formula unit and \(i = 3\):
\(\mathrm{K_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K^+} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)

Using \(\Pi V = i\,n_B\,RT\) with \(n_B = \dfrac{0.025}{174}\), \(V = 2\) L and \(T = 27 + 273 = 300\) K,
\(\Pi = \dfrac{3 \times 0.025 \times 0.082 \times 300}{174 \times 2}\)
\(\Pi = 5.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The temperature must be in kelvin, and the factor of 3 is what the phrase "completely dissociated" is there to supply.

(ii) A maximum boiling azeotrope. Acetone and chloroform show NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law, because a hydrogen bond forms between the hydrogen of chloroform and the carbonyl oxygen of acetone, and that new interaction is stronger than the acetone-acetone and chloroform-chloroform interactions it replaces. The molecules are therefore held in the liquid more tightly than before mixing, fewer escape, the vapour pressure falls below the predicted value, and a mixture with a lowered vapour pressure must be heated further to boil.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) (I) Why do transition metals show variable oxidation states ?
(II) Out of \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ti^{2+}}\) which will be more paramagnetic and why ? [Atomic No. : Ti = 22, Mn = 25]
(III) Which ion is the strongest oxidising agent in the options given below :
\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\)
Give reason.
[Atomic No. : Cr = 24, V = 23, Mn = 25]
(ii) Complete and balance the following equations :
(I) \(\mathrm{2MnO_2 + 4KOH + O_2 \longrightarrow}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{5C_2O_4^{2-} + 2MnO_4^{-} + 16H^{+} \longrightarrow}\)
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Because in a transition metal the \(ns\) and \((n-1)d\) orbitals are very close in energy, so electrons from both can take part in bonding. Different numbers of electrons may be lost depending on the conditions, and the resulting oxidation states usually differ by one — unlike the main group elements, where the inner shell is too far below in energy to be touched.

(II) \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is the more paramagnetic. Manganese has 25 electrons, so \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\) with five unpaired electrons; titanium has 22, so \(\mathrm{Ti^{2+}}\) is \(3d^2\) with only two. Paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons.

(III) \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is the strongest oxidising agent. A strong oxidising agent is one that is readily reduced, and \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^4\), gains the specially stable half-filled \(3d^5\) arrangement by accepting a single electron. \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\), already a stable half-filled \(t_{2g}\) set, and \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) is \(3d^2\); neither has that incentive.

(ii)(I) Fusing manganese dioxide with alkali in air oxidises manganese from \(+4\) to \(+6\), giving the green manganate:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(II) Permanganate oxidises oxalate to carbon dioxide in acid and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\):
\(5\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O} + 10\mathrm{CO_2}\)

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) What is meant by lanthanoid contraction ?
(ii) Why do transition metals form coloured compounds ?
(iii) Why are \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values for Mn and Zn more negative than expected ?
(iv) Which is the most stable oxidation state of Cu and why ?
(v) Why is \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) in aqueous solution a good oxidising agent ?
rows.solution:
(i) Lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series from lanthanum to lutetium. It happens because each added electron goes into a 4f orbital, and f electrons shield the outer electrons from the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge felt by the outermost shell grows steadily and pulls it in. The cumulative effect is large enough that the elements following the series, such as hafnium, are almost the same size as those directly above them.

(ii) Because their ions have partly filled d subshells. The ligands or surrounding ions split the five d orbitals into sets of different energy, and an electron can absorb a photon of visible light to move from a lower set to a higher one. The colour seen is the complement of the light absorbed in this d-d transition. Ions with an empty or a completely filled d subshell, such as \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) or \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), are colourless for want of such a transition.

(iii) Because of the special stability of the ions that are formed. \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\), a half-filled subshell, and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\), a completely filled one. Both arrangements are unusually stable, so the metal gives up its two electrons more readily than the general trend would suggest, and the electrode potential is correspondingly more negative than expected.

(iv) \(+2\) is the most stable oxidation state of copper in aqueous solution. Forming \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) costs a second ionisation enthalpy, but \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is much smaller and more highly charged than \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\), so its hydration enthalpy is far more negative — enough to more than repay that cost. This is why \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) disproportionates in water into \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) and copper metal.

(v) Because \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) reverts to \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\), which is the common and stable oxidation state of the whole lanthanoid series. Being reduced is therefore strongly favoured, and a species readily reduced is by definition a good oxidising agent; ceric ammonium sulphate is used as an oxidant in volumetric analysis for exactly this reason.

rows.stem:
(i) (I) Which of the following is more reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction :
2-Bromo-2-methylbutane or 1-Bromopentane
(II) What type of halide is present in the following compound :
\(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH(CH_3) - C(Cl) = CH_2}\)
(III) Why is chloroform stored in dark coloured bottles ?
(ii) Define the following terms :
(I) Ambident Nucleophiles
(II) Racemic mixture
rows.solution:
(i)(I) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is the more reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N}1\). That reaction goes through a carbocation, and 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is a tertiary halide whose cation is stabilised by three alkyl groups. 1-Bromopentane is primary, and a primary carbocation is too unstable to form, so it reacts by the \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) route instead.

(II) It is a vinylic halide. The chlorine is attached directly to a carbon that is part of a carbon-carbon double bond, and that is what defines a vinylic halide. Such halides are very unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution, for the same reason as aryl halides: the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond has partial double bond character and the carbon is \(sp^2\).

(III) Because chloroform is slowly oxidised by atmospheric oxygen in the presence of light to phosgene, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\), which is extremely poisonous:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)
Dark coloured glass excludes the light, and the bottles are also filled to the brim so as to exclude the air.

(ii)(I) An ambident nucleophile is a nucleophile that has two different nucleophilic centres and can attack through either one, giving two different products. The cyanide ion is the standard example: attacking through carbon gives an alkyl cyanide and through nitrogen an alkyl isocyanide. The nitrite ion behaves the same way, through nitrogen or through oxygen.

(II) A racemic mixture is an equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers of a compound, the \(d\) and \(l\) forms. Their optical rotations are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so they cancel exactly and the mixture is optically inactive.

rows.stem:
(i) Answer the following :
(I) Which isomer of \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\) is most reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction ?
(II) Predict the alkene that would be formed by dehydrohalogenation of 1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.
(III) Although chlorine shows strong – I effect, yet it is ortho/para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions. Why ?
(ii) Write the major product in the following reactions :
(I) \(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na/dry\ Ether}}\)
(II) 4-nitrocumene \(\mathrm{(O_2N - C_6H_4 - CH(CH_3)_2}\), para\()\) + \(\mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — both reactions of part (ii) are printed as SKELETAL DRAWINGS and the stem (‘Write the major product in the following reactions :’) names nothing on its own: (I) is ‘2’ followed by a plain benzene hexagon bonded to Cl; (II) is a benzene hexagon carrying \(\mathrm{CH(CH_3)_2}\) with \(\mathrm{O_2N}\) drawn on the PARA carbon, plus \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) over a ‘heat’ arrow. Both compounds are named losslessly in the stem (chlorobenzene; 4-nitrocumene), so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) The tertiary isomer, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}\). An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction proceeds through a carbocation, and three alkyl groups stabilise that cation better than any other arrangement of \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\) can.

(II) Dehydrohalogenation removes the bromine together with a hydrogen from an adjacent carbon, and here that hydrogen may come either from a ring carbon or from the methyl group. Taking a ring hydrogen gives the more substituted and therefore more stable alkene, and by Saytzeff's rule that is the major product: 1-methylcyclohexene, with the double bond inside the ring. Methylenecyclohexane is the minor product.

(III) The two effects of chlorine answer different questions. Its \(-I\) effect withdraws electron density from the whole ring and slows every electrophilic substitution, so chlorobenzene is less reactive than benzene. But chlorine's lone pairs give it a \(+R\) effect, which builds up electron density at the ortho and para positions specifically; attack there produces a carbocation intermediate with an extra resonance structure in which chlorine carries the positive charge, and meta attack has no such structure. So the RATE is set by \(-I\) and the POSITION by \(+R\).

(ii)(I) This is the Fittig reaction, the aryl analogue of Wurtz coupling. Sodium in dry ether couples two aryl halide units through the carbons that carried the halogen:
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)
The product is biphenyl.

(II) Bromine with heat attacks the side chain rather than the ring, and within the side chain it takes the benzylic hydrogen — the one on the carbon attached to the ring — because the radical formed there is stabilised by the ring. In 4-nitrocumene that carbon is the tertiary \(\mathrm{CH}\) of the isopropyl group, which is benzylic and tertiary at once:
\(\mathrm{4\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CH(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{4\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CBr(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{HBr}\)
The product is 2-bromo-2-(4-nitrophenyl)propane. The nitro group deactivates the ring, which makes side-chain attack the more favourable route still.
